screens.title: Documenting Architectural Decisions (ADRs)
screens.narratorSegment: Architectural Decision Records, or ADRs, are compact documents that explain why a team chose one architectural path over others. They capture the context, the options considered, the concrete decision, and its consequences. ADRs turn transient conversations into discoverable history: when team members change or months pass, the reasoning remains. That matters because architectural choices often depend on constraints that shift slowly — team skills, performance targets, operational capabilities — and without a record, teams risk undoing important trade-offs. In this lesson you will see how ADRs are structured, when to write them, and how to keep them useful over time. We'll explore concrete examples, a writing template, and practical tips for integrating ADRs into your version control workflow with tools that streamline creation. By the end you should be able to decide which decisions deserve an ADR, draft one that is concise and actionable, and place it where future readers will find it. Think about a recent decision you made at work: would a short ADR have prevented a later question or rework? That's the power we're building toward.

screens.title: What is an ADR?
screens.narratorSegment: An Architectural Decision Record, or ADR, is a short document that records a single significant architectural decision, why it was made, what options were considered, and what consequences follow. The ADR's purpose is to preserve the context and reasoning so future readers can understand the original forces at play. For example, a team might write an ADR titled 'Use PostgreSQL for Primary Data Store' with context describing write load and geospatial needs, options like MySQL or MongoDB, a clear decision, and consequences such as required training. ADRs are intentionally lightweight: they should be focused enough to answer questions later without long narrative. A common misconception is that ADRs replace design diagrams; they do not. Instead, ADRs complement architectural views by explaining the rationale behind choices in words. That makes ADRs particularly useful during onboarding, retrospectives, or when evaluating a refactor. When you write an ADR, aim for clarity: state the problem, list viable alternatives, explain why the selected option fits this problem now, and note both positive and negative consequences. Would a later reader be able to decide whether the original assumptions still apply? If yes, your ADR did its job.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.6 › What is an ADR?
Definition & purpose
ADRs record a single architectural decision with context, options, rationale, and consequences so future teams understand the reasoning.
Concrete example
Title: Use PostgreSQL for Primary Data Store. Context: high write load and geospatial queries. Decision: Adopt PostgreSQL. Consequences: training, migration effort.
Common misconception
ADRs don't replace diagrams; they explain why the diagram looks the way it does and what assumptions underlie it.
Key Takeaway

ADRs are compact decision journals that make architectural reasoning discoverable and durable.

Annotated ADR Template
Title • Status • Context • Decision • Options Considered • Rationale • Consequences
Each section answers a reader question: what happened, why, and what follows.
Example card
If you see 'Superseded' status later, link to the ADR that replaced it so the history is clear.
Pro tip
Keep ADRs short and focused; a few paragraphs per section is usually enough.

screens.title: Typical ADR Structure
screens.narratorSegment: A typical ADR follows a simple sequence that guides a reader from problem to outcome. Start with a concise Title that names the decision and a Status that shows whether it is proposed, accepted, superseded, or deprecated. Next, describe the Context: the problem, constraints, and forces that made the decision necessary. Then state the Decision itself clearly and unambiguously so there is no doubt about the chosen course. After that, list Options Considered — even briefly — to demonstrate due diligence. The Rationale explains why the chosen option best fits the context; include benefits and drawbacks. Finally, record the Consequences: both positive and negative impacts on development, operations, and future change. For example, if you choose PostgreSQL, the rationale might cite PostGIS support and write performance, while consequences include team training and migration effort. A good process for writing ADRs is to capture the decision as it happens, list alternatives, write a concise rationale, and commit the ADR into docs/arch/decisions in version control. That habit keeps ADRs current and discoverable. Typical ADR Structure means follow title → status → context → decision → options → rationale → consequences to tell a clear decision story.. In practical terms, a reliable order to tell the decision story. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.6 › Typical ADR Structure
Linear writing flow
Use this ordered template to reduce reader friction and make assumptions explicit.
1
Title & Status
A precise name and a clear status so readers know if the decision is current.
2
Context
What problem and constraints led to this decision. Include measurable expectations if possible.
3
Decision & Options
State the decision clearly and list alternatives considered so readers see the trade space.
4
Rationale & Consequences
Explain why this option fits and record expected positive and negative impacts to guide future change.
Example sequence
Title: Use PostgreSQL. Status: Accepted. Context: high write loads, geospatial queries. Decision: adopt PostgreSQL. Options: MySQL, MongoDB, CockroachDB. Rationale: PostGIS, indexing. Consequences: migration work and training.
Check your writing
  • Is the decision unambiguous?
  • Are alternatives listed, even briefly?
  • Do consequences include operational impacts?

screens.title: Which decisions need ADRs?
screens.narratorSegment: Not every design choice deserves an ADR. The idea is to capture decisions that are consequential, difficult to reverse, or involve cross-cutting trade-offs. Concluding that a color palette should change does not need an ADR, but selecting an architectural style — microservices versus monolith — almost certainly does. Other ADR-worthy topics include selecting a messaging backbone, authentication strategy, data storage mechanism, or an infrastructure approach that changes operations. ADRs are most valuable when the decision depends on assumptions that may later be questioned, such as team skills, expected scale, or regulatory constraints. A useful way to decide is to ask: will someone need to know why this was chosen in a year? If the answer is yes, write an ADR. Common mistakes are either over-documenting trivial choices or under-documenting major trade-offs. The correct balance keeps ADRs concise, focused on decisions that matter, and integrated with the team's completion criteria so documentation actually happens while context is fresh. Which decisions need ADRs? means write adrs for impactful, hard-to-reverse, or cross-cutting decisions; avoid documenting trivial, easily changed preferences.. In practical terms, choose where to invest documentation effort. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Decision filters
Use quick filters to decide if an ADR is warranted.
Impact
Does the decision affect many teams, releases, or operational processes?
Reversibility
Is reversing this decision costly or risky? If yes, document it.
Assumptions

Examples that need ADRs

Common mistake

screens.title: Consequences and Operational Impact
screens.narratorSegment: Consequences are the section of an ADR where you make the decision's practical impact explicit. Positive consequences show benefits: improved query performance, better scaling, or reduced latency. Negative consequences record costs and risks: increased operational complexity, required team training, migration effort, or vendor lock-in. Including both sides helps stakeholders and future engineers assess the trade-off and decide whether the original assumptions still hold. A good consequence statement is concrete: instead of saying 'may increase complexity', say 'requires two weeks of team training and introduces a new database to operations'. This specificity makes refactors and audits faster because readers can estimate the real cost of change. A common misconception is to bury long implementation details in consequences; keep consequences focused on impact, not the full migration plan. If actions are required, link to a follow-up ADR or a migration plan rather than expanding the consequences section into tasks. Clear consequences guide future decisions about whether to keep, modify, or replace the original choice. In practical terms, capture the positive and negative outcomes that matter to teams. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Why consequences matter
Consequences translate an abstract choice into operational realities that teams must manage.
Positive consequence example
Improved geospatial query performance enabling richer mapping features.
Negative consequence example
Requires two weeks of training and increases operational complexity with a new database type.
How to write consequences
  • Be specific and measurable where possible.
  • Separate operational costs from development impacts.
  • Link to related ADRs or migration plans when appropriate.
Check your consequences
If someone can estimate time or risk from your consequence statements, you are providing useful guidance for future decisions.

screens.title: Managing ADRs in a Project
screens.narratorSegment: Good ADR management ensures decision history is accessible and maintained. Store ADRs alongside code in a predictable folder, for example docs/arch/decisions, so contributors find them during code review or feature work. Use version control to track changes, set the ADR file name to include a short identifier and title, and update Status when a decision is accepted or superseded. Integrate ADR creation into your workflow: make writing an ADR part of the completion criteria for tasks that involve significant architectural choices. Tools like adr-tools can create a new ADR file and help with standardized headers, which reduces friction. Another recommendation is to link ADRs from design documents and pull requests so reviewers can easily find the reasoning behind choices. Finally, treat ADRs as living documents — add a superseding ADR if the decision changes instead of editing history away. This practice preserves the evolution of thinking and prevents losing the assumptions that led earlier teams to their choice. Module 07 › Chapter 7.6 › Managing ADRs in a Project
Storage pattern
Place ADRs in docs/arch/decisions and commit them with related feature or architectural work.
Versioning and status
Keep status up to date: Proposed, Accepted, Superseded, Deprecated. If something changes, add a new ADR with a link to the previous one to preserve history.
Tooling and workflow
Use small tools to scaffold ADR files and integrate ADR writing into pull requests and code reviews to reduce friction.
Practical checklist
  • ADR in docs/arch/decisions
  • Link ADR in PR and design docs
  • Update status when superseded

screens.title: Using adr-tools and Git
screens.narratorSegment: Simple tooling reduces friction when creating ADRs. Tools such as adr-tools provide a tiny scaffold so authors can create a new ADR file with a standard header and filename. The key habit is to commit the ADR into docs/arch/decisions in the same repository where the code lives. When a decision is made during a task, run the scaffolding command to create the file, fill in the sections, and push a commit along with your code changes. This ensures the reason for the change is discoverable in the pull request and the ADR history is versioned. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Living Documents

Architectural Decision Records, or ADRs, are compact documents that explain why a team chose one architectural path over others. They capture the context, the options considered, the concrete decision, and its consequences. ADRs turn transient conversations into discoverable history: when team members change or months pass, the reasoning remains. That matters because architectural choices often depend on constraints that shift slowly — team skills, performance targets, operational capabilities — and without a record, teams risk undoing important trade-offs. In this lesson you will see how ADRs are structured, when to write them, and how to keep them useful over time. We'll explore concrete examples, a writing template, and practical tips for integrating ADRs into your version control workflow with tools that streamline creation. By the end you should be able to decide which decisions deserve an ADR, draft one that is concise and actionable, and place it where future readers will find it. Think about a recent decision you made at work: would a short ADR have prevented a later question or rework? That's the power we're building toward.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why ADRs matter, identify when to capture a decision, and write concise, actionable ADRs that future readers can use. You will learn the canonical ADR structure — title, status, context, decision, options, rationale, and consequences — and how each part contributes to clarity. You will also practice choosing which decisions require an ADR versus those better kept as lightweight notes. Importantly, you'll learn how to store ADRs in version control and use simple tools to create and track them so they are discoverable and versioned alongside code. Finally, you'll see how to integrate ADR writing into your team's workflow so documentation happens as part of completion, not as an afterthought. Each objective links to practical skills: drafting an ADR, evaluating trade-offs, and maintaining living documents when circumstances change. Keeping these skills current prevents costly rework and preserves institutional memory.

Each objective includes a compact mnemonic or visual pattern to help you remember the structure and placement of an ADR within a repository. These skills improve team alignment and make future architectural changes safer and faster because decision history is explicit and discoverable rather than scattered in meeting notes or abandoned tickets.

An Architectural Decision Record, or ADR, is a short document that records a single significant architectural decision, why it was made, what options were considered, and what consequences follow. The ADR's purpose is to preserve the context and reasoning so future readers can understand the original forces at play. For example, a team might write an ADR titled 'Use PostgreSQL for Primary Data Store' with context describing write load and geospatial needs, options like MySQL or MongoDB, a clear decision, and consequences such as required training. ADRs are intentionally lightweight: they should be focused enough to answer questions later without long narrative. A common misconception is that ADRs replace design diagrams; they do not. Instead, ADRs complement architectural views by explaining the rationale behind choices in words. That makes ADRs particularly useful during onboarding, retrospectives, or when evaluating a refactor. When you write an ADR, aim for clarity: state the problem, list viable alternatives, explain why the selected option fits this problem now, and note both positive and negative consequences. Would a later reader be able to decide whether the original assumptions still apply? If yes, your ADR did its job.

A typical ADR follows a simple sequence that guides a reader from problem to outcome. Start with a concise Title that names the decision and a Status that shows whether it is proposed, accepted, superseded, or deprecated. Next, describe the Context: the problem, constraints, and forces that made the decision necessary. Then state the Decision itself clearly and unambiguously so there is no doubt about the chosen course. After that, list Options Considered — even briefly — to demonstrate due diligence. The Rationale explains why the chosen option best fits the context; include benefits and drawbacks. Finally, record the Consequences: both positive and negative impacts on development, operations, and future change. For example, if you choose PostgreSQL, the rationale might cite PostGIS support and write performance, while consequences include team training and migration effort. A good process for writing ADRs is to capture the decision as it happens, list alternatives, write a concise rationale, and commit the ADR into docs/arch/decisions in version control. Not every design choice deserves an ADR. The idea is to capture decisions that are consequential, difficult to reverse, or involve cross-cutting trade-offs.
